catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ponce-de-leon: Ponce de León was the conquistador who sought the Fountain of Youth and found Florida. This entry traces his voyages, his governorship, and his death. The discoverer of the Flowery Land: his fabled fountain proved a cruel mirage at last.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-conon: Conon was the Sicilian pope of 687, old and sick at his election. This entry notes his brief pontificate and the scant records. The venerable elder of the seventh century: his peaceful election pleased all the warring Roman factions at once.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-porphyreon: Porphyreon was a city of ancient Phoenicia important enough to host a Christian bishop, and its see survives today only as a titular one. This brief entry notes its site and its early church history. A quiet name from the Levantine coast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-postcommunion: The Postcommunion is the Mass prayer after the faithful have received. This entry explains its form, its history, and its meaning. The thanksgiving of the sacred banquet: its brief prayer seals the holy Mass each day worldwide in ancient Latin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-postulation: Postulation is the canonical petition for a dispensation or favor. This entry explains its kinds, its procedure, and its effects. The Church's formal asking: its humble petitions seek the pope's gracious favor in eternal Rome itself today still heard gladly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pragmatic-san: The Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges asserted the French Church's liberties. This entry explains its articles, its fate, and its significance. The charter of Gallicanism: its bold articles curbed the distant pope in Rome itself in 1438's hot July days of Bourges.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-preconization: Preconization is the consistory's formal naming of a bishop. This entry explains its rite, its history, and its law. The pope's public choice: its solemn rite names the chosen bishop-elect in papal Rome itself in solemn consistory hall today still.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-predestinatio: Predestination is God's eternal decree of the elect's glory. This long entry examines its mystery, its schools, and the Catholic doctrine. The secret of the chosen: its awful mystery humbles the proudest human mind to lowly dust in holy awe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prescription: Prescription is the moral theologian's term for rights acquired by time. This entry explains its conditions, its kinds, and its applications. The theology of time's title: its silent years vest the hidden right in moral conscience at last in peace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presumption: Presumption is the sin of rash hope in God's mercy. This entry explains its kinds, its gravity, and its remedies. The counterfeit of true hope: its blind rashness offends a holy and just heaven itself in foolish pride and folly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-promulgation: Promulgation is the publication that makes a law binding. This entry explains its forms, its necessity, and its effects. The birth of the law: its solemn act makes the dead statute live at last in binding force of holy law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psalms-of-sol: The Psalms of Solomon are the apocryphal hymns of the Pharisees' age. This entry examines their origin, their contents, and their value. The songs of the Hasidim: their fervent hope awaited the promised Messiah in prayer and fasting and tears.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psychological: Psychological assimilation is the mind's digestion of new knowledge. This entry explains its process and its place in teaching. The learning that becomes one's own: its quiet digestion feeds the growing mind in school each passing day in turn unbroken.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quilon: Quilon became the diocese of India's Malabar coast. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history as of 1913. The faith on the pepper coast: its old churches dot the Kerala lagoons in India's sunny south in living faith today.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ratisbon: Ratisbon became the diocese of Regensburg. This entry covers its bishops, churches, and history. The faith on the Danube's north bank: its twin-towered cathedral crowns the old city of Ratisbon in Bavaria's green heart of faith and ancient stone and prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-breto: Raymond Breton was the Dominican missionary of the Caribs. This entry notes his grammar, his missions, and his labors. The apostle of Guadeloupe: his great dictionary saved the Carib language from oblivion in printed form forevermore in print and ink.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-caron: Raymond Caron was the Irish Franciscan theologian. This entry notes his works, his teaching, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A quiet name of the Friars Minor: his subtle theses filled the Irish schools of theology in Louvain.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reason: Reason is the mind's power of knowing truth. This long entry examines its nature, its rights, and its relation to faith. The lamp of the intellect: its clear light serves the Catholic faith in truth and charity and hope and reason.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-recollection: Recollection is the gathering of the mind into God's presence. This entry explains its practice, its degrees, and its fruits. The silence that finds the Guest: its daily habit stills the restless soul in quiet prayer and holy peace and love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-redemption: Redemption is Christ's buying back of fallen man. This long entry examines its nature, its price, and its fruits. The ransom of the world: its precious blood bought the sinful slaves of Satan and sin and death and hell itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regeneration: Regeneration is the new birth of baptism. This entry examines its nature, its effects, and its theology. The washing of the second birth: its cleansing water renews the sinful soul in baptismal grace and light and life eternal and new.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religion: Religion is man's bond with God expressed in worship. This long entry examines its nature, its history, and its necessity. The virtue that honors the divine: its true worship crowns the humble soul with grace and peace and joy and light.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-con: The Congregations of the Presentation are the sisterhoods of Mary's feast. This entry notes their foundations, their schools, and their works. The daughters of the Presentation: their quiet convents dot the dioceses of France and beyond the seas in prayer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-of-: The Religious of Perpetual Adoration are the adorers of the Host. This entry notes their foundation, their rule, and their houses. The watchers before the tabernacle: their holy hours never cease day or night in prayer and praise and song.

The Religious of the Perpetual Adoration are the sisters of the endless praise. This entry notes their houses, their rule, and their devotion. The choir that never sleeps: their endless praise fills the night with song and prayer and love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-pro: Religious profession is the solemn taking of the vows. This entry explains its kinds, its effects, and its rite. The marriage to Christ: its solemn vows bind the soul to Christ forever in love and fidelity and joy and peace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-tol: Religious toleration is the state's patience with differing faiths. This entry examines its principle, its limits, and the Catholic doctrine. The peace of the mixed city: its civil law permits the sects to worship in peace and quiet and order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-edouard-: René-Édouard Caron was the Quebec jurist and lieutenant-governor. This entry notes his career, his offices, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A French-Canadian statesman: his judicial robes graced the bench of Quebec's courts in the 1800s' decades.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-renunciation: Renunciation is the giving up of a right or office. This entry explains its kinds, its conditions, and its effects. The surrender of the claim: its solemn act frees the office for another's hands in law and peace and order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reparation: Reparation is the making amends to the Sacred Heart. This entry explains its devotion, its practices, and its theology. The atonement of the loving heart: its holy hours console the Heart of Jesus in love and tears and prayer and song.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reservation: Reservation is the pope's keeping of benefices to himself. This entry explains its kinds, its history, and its law. The papal hold on the appointment: its ancient right names the bishop of Rome's choice in conclave's vote of scarlet cardinals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-restitution: Restitution is the paying back of what was unjustly taken. This entry examines its obligation, its measure, and its theology. The repair of the stolen good: its stern debt binds the conscience till paid in full and just measure of right.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-revelation: Revelation is God's speaking to man of Himself. This long entry examines its nature, its modes, and its completion. The divine unveiling of truth: its living word ends in Christ Jesus our Lord and King and God and Man and Savior.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-revocation: Revocation is the withdrawing of a grant or privilege. This entry explains its kinds, its conditions, and its effects. The recall of the favor: its formal decree annuls the papal grant in law and fact and right and deed and name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-angel: Richard Angelus Mason was the English Franciscan of the penal years. This entry notes his career, his works, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A friar of the hidden church: his brown habit braved the penal laws.

dombey-and-son: Dickens's 1848 novel about proud Mr. Dombey, who values his son as a business heir and neglects his loving daughter Florence. drusilla-with-a-million: Elizabeth Cooper's lighthearted novel follows Drusilla, whose sudden million turns her quiet life upside down. Fortune-hunters, social climbers, and one honest suitor compete for her hand — and her heart must sort them out. A merry, old-fashioned comedy of wealth and love.
eight-years-wanderings-in-ceylon: Samuel White Baker's account of eight years in Ceylon: big-game hunting, coffee planting, and colonial life. epictetus-discourses-enchiridion-matheso:
Epictetus, a Greek slave in Rome who won his freedom and taught philosophy, left no writings of his own. His pupil Arrian took notes on his talks, which became the Discourses, and boiled the teaching into the Enchiridion, or Handbook. P. E. Matheson's 1916 translation covers both, the four books of Discourses and the short Handbook.

Epictetus teaches that some things are up to us and others are not, and peace lies in knowing the split. Wealth, health, and fame sit outside our power; our judgments and choices sit inside it. His voice is blunt, funny, and practical. The Handbook became a pocket guide carried by soldiers and emperors alike.
erewhon:
Samuel Butler, an English writer with a sharp wit, wrote this satire of a made up land in 1872. Erewhon is 'nowhere' spelled near back to front, a hint of the game he plays. Butler had lived in New Zealand, and the land of his book owes much to that stay.

In Erewhon, machines are banned as a risk to man, and sick men are tried as rogues. Health is a crime and crime is a disease to be cured, in a world turned on its head. The mirror shows Victorian England its own face, and the joke still cuts deep.
fanny-campbell-the-female-pirate-captain: Fanny Campbell, the Female Pirate Captain, a tale of the Revolution. The lady pirate. This book preserves that adventure. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
five-lectures-on-reincarnation: Swami Abhedananda lectures on reincarnation — the soul's long pilgrimage through many lives — with Vedantic clarity. from-the-earth-to-the-moon-and-round-the: Verne's 1865 From the Earth to the Moon fires a cannon shell at the Moon. Science fiction launched. The Tower library holds the full text. It aimed at Luna. garuda-purana-basu-edition:
Publisher B. D. Basu issued the Garuda Purana in his Sacred Books of the Hindus series. Sanskrit scholars rendered the old text into English for the set. In the Purana, the bird god Garuda questions Vishnu.

Their talk covers creation, worship, gems, medicine, and law. Long sections dwell on death, judgment, and the soul's path after it. Rites for the dead get careful, full detail. The book blends lore that is practical and cosmic at once. It remains a key source for Hindu teaching on dying and what may follow.
george-silverman-s-explanation: A late Dickens story narrated by a clergyman explaining a life shaped by childhood poverty and misunderstanding. Quiet, sad, and psychologically subtle, it is unlike the author's boisterous novels. Published in 1868, it shows Dickens experimenting with a restrained, confessional voice near the end of his career.
govdocs-archive_org-SeptuagintBrenton185:
A second holding of Brenton's Septuagint sits beside the first: the same 1851 English translation of the Greek Old Testament, published in London by Samuel Bagster and Sons. Duplicate copies are kept because scans can differ in quality and completeness.

The text gives the full Septuagint with the Apocrypha, the ancient Greek scriptures that shaped the early church and much of the New Testament's language. Brenton worked directly from the Greek and produced the English version readers used for over a century. Having two captures lets readers check a doubtful page in one copy against the other.
govdocs-archive_org-TheUnitedStatesInFor:
Walter Lippmann, the most influential American newspaper columnist of his era, wrote this 1932 account of American foreign relations. He prepared it with the research staff of the Council on Foreign Relations, and Harper and Brothers published it for the Council.

The book surveys a single year of United States dealings with the world, in Lippmann's clear and measured style. It belonged to an annual series meant to give citizens a reliable map of foreign policy between the world wars. Readers today get both the facts of 1932 diplomacy and a model of how public argument about it was once done.
govdocs-archive_org-US-Government-Medica:
In 1975 two Senate subcommittees, on Health and on Administrative Practice and Procedure, held joint hearings on biomedical and behavioral research. Their subject was human experimentation run by the Department of Defense and the Central Intelligence Agency, programs then coming into public view.

Witnesses and documents laid out drug and behavior experiments on people, the territory of MKULTRA and the Edgewood Arsenal tests. The hearings also took up bill S. 2515, which would create a presidential commission to protect human subjects in research. The transcript is Congress's oversight record at the moment the secret programs were forced into the open.
govdocs-archive_org-eedDouglasTheControv:
Douglas Reed, a former Times correspondent who covered Central Europe before the Second World War, wrote The Controversy of Zion between 1951 and 1956. No publisher took the manuscript for two decades; it first appeared in 1978, from Dolphin Press of Durban.

Reed presents his history of Zionism as a political project reaching from ancient times to the modern state of Israel, told in conspiratorial terms across the centuries. The book is his largest work, and the one his reputation now rests on. It is hotly debated and held as an archive item, without endorsement, for readers of postwar political literature.
govdocs-archive_org-media-argumentation_:
Media Argumentation is a scholarly book on how arguments work in public communication. It approaches its subject from informal logic, the branch of logic that studies real arguments as people actually make them, rather than formal proofs.

The book covers dialectic and rhetoric, the catalog of argumentation schemes speakers rely on, and the mechanics of persuasion and social influence. Its question throughout is how media messages argue, and how audiences should judge those arguments. It is a learned work, meant for students of communication and argumentation theory in the communications age.

Weisberg's correspondence files grew enormous over the decades, as witnesses, researchers, and the merely curious wrote to him about the case. A single incoming letter like this one is a thread in that web: private citizens exchanging what they knew and suspected. The letter is kept as part of the research correspondence preserved in the archive.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AndersonHaroldG:
MURKIN was the FBI's case name for the investigation of the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. This urgent teletype came from the Bureau's Atlanta office on May 27, 1968, seven weeks after the shooting in Memphis.

By then the hunt centered on James Earl Ray, whose fingerprints had tied him to the rifle and the rooming house, and who was still at large overseas. Teletypes were the Bureau's nervous system during the manhunt, moving sightings and orders between offices by the hour. The file is a page of that traffic, preserved as issued for researchers of the King case.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AngletonJames_J: James Jesus Angleton ran the CIA's counterintelligence staff for twenty years and became the agency's legendary mole hunter, convinced a Soviet penetration sat at the heart of American intelligence. This file holds the government material filed under his name in the assassination-era records. The file is kept as issued, under the name of the most feared spycatcher of the Cold War.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-AutopsyJFKNatio:
On May 26, 1966, a writer addressed a letter to Marlon Johnson of the National Archives about the Kennedy autopsy materials. The letter raises concerns about how those materials were being handled and asks that it be directed to the proper authority.

Custody of the autopsy record was a live fight in 1966, the year the photographs, X-rays, and related materials were formally deposited with the Archives under restrictions. Every transfer raised questions about who controlled the evidence, and letters from researchers pressed for answers. Preserved in the files, this letter shows that pressure arriving while the arrangements were still being settled.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-CottonStampPlan:
Writing on April 30, 1940, Harold Weisberg answered a query from Helen Kay in a letter addressed to Cameron. The subject was the cotton stamp plan, a New Deal-era program, and a set of lisle hose samples made in a government style. Weisberg enclosed the samples with his reply.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DelgadoNelson_D:
Nelson Delgado knew Lee Harvey Oswald in the Marine Corps, which made him a witness investigators wanted to hear at length. A long deposition transcript preserves Delgado's sworn answers. The questioning moves exhibit by exhibit, and the body that took the deposition is not identified in the text.

Delgado's value as a witness came from daily contact with Oswald in service. Men who trained and bunked beside him could describe his habits, skills, and talk in a way later witnesses could not. A transcript of this length lets readers weigh his account in full, question by question, instead of in short quoted pieces.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FBICorruption_F:
Charles R. Babcock reported for the Washington Post on a Justice Department report with embarrassing findings. The report charged that J. Edgar Hoover and his aides had misused FBI employees, equipment, and funds for personal service. The Bureau's own parent department had documented a pattern of abuses at the top.

Hoover had run the FBI for decades as a power beyond easy challenge. A formal finding that he treated staff and public money as his own cut at that legend. Babcock's article preserves the charges as they were made public, a rare official reckoning with Hoover's rule.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ITEKCorporation:
Itek Corporation, an optics firm, analyzed the film of the Kennedy assassination for Life magazine. Its analysis is dated November 20, 1967, four years after the shooting. Life held the Zapruder film, and it hired technical experts to study what the frames could prove.

Film analysis turned a home movie into measured evidence: timing, motion, and sequence read frame by frame. Itek's work for Life was among the most serious early efforts of that kind. The report preserves laboratory methods applied to the most argued-over strip of film in America, work done for a magazine rather than a court.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MartensLaytonPa:
An FBI memorandum dated March 8, 1967 concerns Layton Patrick Martens, born February 19, 1943. It was filed under 'Assassination of President Kennedy, Dallas, Texas.' Copies were routed to a row of senior officials: DeLoach, Malley, Wick, Jonsen, Sullivan, Rosen, and Branigan.

The routing list is itself the news. A memo about a 24-year-old man reached the bureau's top floor because every name near the case was handled at that level. Martens appears in the New Orleans side of the inquiry, where investigators were tracing the city's anti-Castro and student circles. The memorandum preserves the bureau's handling of one such name: dated, copied upward, and kept.

The New Orleans States-Item reported on September 13, 1972, that Dr. Alton Ochsner was to be honored. The honor came from the Information Council of the Americas, known as INCA. Headquarters, 1st Marine Aircraft Wing issued these records of Operation Strongback on January 31, 1958. The wing operated as CTG 71.3 for the exercise. Decades later, in 1992, the records were obtained from the National Records Center, where old military paper goes to rest.

Operation records of this kind list units, movements, orders, and reports for a single exercise. Strongback was a Cold War training operation in the Pacific, part of the rehearsal of American power in Asia. The file's survival path is part of its interest: created by a headquarters staff in 1958, stored by the government, and pulled by a researcher thirty-four years later under its operation name.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Personal-Nixon_:
William Chapman, a Washington Post staff writer, wrote this article about Harry Truman's dislikes. Its title is 'Truman Couldn't Stand Nixon.' Truman, the story says, held generals in low regard, naming Eisenhower and MacArthur. Richard Nixon was one of only two people in the country Truman absolutely could not stand.

Truman's plain talk stayed quotable long after his presidency. Chapman collects the former president's judgments on the men who followed and opposed him. The Nixon line carries the piece: two Missourians of opposite parties, divided by the scandals of 1950s politics. The article is political portraiture by quotation, and it preserves Truman's voice as Washington remembered it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Revolucion_Revo:
The Cuban newspaper Revolución printed Fidel Castro's address on the Kennedy assassination. Castro spoke on television and radio on a Saturday night, addressing Cuba directly. He spoke about the assassination and about what he called the campaign of reactionary hysteria around it. The paper gives the full text of his remarks, as rendered by the Department of Versions of the Revolutionary Government.

Castro had reason to fear the aftermath: early reports tied Oswald to Cuba, and invasion talk rose at once. His address answered that danger in public. The official rendering matters, because it is the version Havana chose to print. Readers get Castro's argument as his government fixed it, a primary text of the crisis from the island's side.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WashingtonianMa: Diana McLellan marked a birthday for Washingtonian magazine with an article titled Well-Heeled, Can't Dance. The piece looks back at the magazine's tenth anniversary and its founding in 1965. Washingtonian covered the capital's social world, and McLellan was known for her sharp Ear column. The article is a light, insider history of a city magazine and the people who filled its pages.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WilsonCharlesHR: Harold Weisberg wrote to Representative Charles H. Wilson of California on August 2, 1975. Weisberg often asked members of Congress to press agencies for records or answers. A letter to a sitting congressman was one of his standard tools. The Wilson letter keeps that pattern in view: a citizen researcher asking elected power to pull on a bureaucracy that would not move for him alone.
govdocs-archive_org-the-essential-mae-br: The Essential Mae Brussell: Investigations of Fascism in America - the essential Mae Brussell collection - the made public government document, subject: government records, a single volume, dated entry, filed.
